items.title: The Essential-Body Verses Open: Avoid All Evil, Abandon All Desire

items.zh: 二涅槃果，增上慧學究竟清淨。聽聞正法，常思惟言，顯示了相作意。常修習言，顯示勝解作意。由起勝解而修習故。先觀見麁靜言，顯示遠離作意。於修習一向等言，顯示攝樂作意。於諸相觀察言，顯示觀察作意。加行究竟言，顯示加行究竟作意。能離欲界欲，及離色界欲，入真諦現觀，能離一切欲等言，顯示世間、出世間加行究竟果作意。
items.en: 'One should arouse diligent effort, always firm and courageous, constantly cultivate heedfulness, and abide well in its five limbs': this verse shows that, through armour-like, applied, and unflagging effort, and through cultivating the five limbs of heedfulness, what is trained becomes pure and excellent. The five limbs of heedfulness concern the past, the future, the present, what was done before, and what is practised together. 'One should hide one's own good deeds and also disclose one's faults; whatever robes and the like one receives, coarse or fine, be glad of them all; be little involved in worldly affairs and get by with what is poor; take up the qualities of the austerities, for calm and freedom from afflictions': these two verses show that the training becomes pure because one leaves behind the causes of desire for followers, of many wants, and of discontent, and leaves behind the causes by which many wants and discontent obstruct pure training. 'One should be complete in deportment, accept things in due measure, and never put on a show of deportment': this verse shows that the training becomes pure because one is complete in deportment; does not put on a false show before others; knows well the measure of whatever one accepts; and accepts things to sustain one's life in order to practise the holy life. 'Do not speak of your own real virtues, nor have others speak of them; though you seek something, do not make a show of special signs; when begging from others, never use force or pressure; obtain things by the Dharma, and having obtained them, do not disparage them': these two verses show that what is trained becomes pure and excellent because one leaves behind flattering talk, false shows, force and pressure, and using what one has gained to attract further gain. 'Do not be attached to gain and respect, and do not cling to views that add or take away': this verse shows that what is trained becomes pure and excellent because one is not attached to gain and respect and does not cling to the five kinds of bad view. 'Do not cling to the worldly-minded, meaningless texts and spells, nor delight in hoarding meaningless spare robes and bowls': this verse shows not clinging to the causes of bad views, the wrong treatises of non-Buddhists, because they obstruct liberation from the aggregates of grasping; what those people compose is called 'worldly-minded'. It also shows leaving behind spare robes, bowls, and the like, which are causes of attachment to gain and respect. Because the causes are pure, the training becomes pure. 'Fearing to increase the afflictions, do not become attached to household life; to purify and cultivate wisdom, keep company with the wise and noble': this verse shows that the training becomes pure because one leaves behind the causes of what is to be counteracted and keeps company with the causes of what counteracts. 'Do not keep households as friends, fearing they will stir up sorrow, grief, and distraction, which give rise to suffering and afflictions; as soon as these arise, leave them behind at once': this verse shows that keeping company with households produces sorrow, grief, and distraction, increases the afflictions, and becomes a cause of many sufferings. Since keeping company with them produces many sufferings, as soon as an affliction arises one dispels it at once; this shows the cause of the counteraction. 'Do not accept the offerings of the faithful, fearing they will harm you like a festering sore; never abandon the Tathāgata's true Dharma': this verse shows not being greedy for gain and respect, not clinging firmly to bad wrong views, not using the offerings of the faithful in vain, and not slandering the true Dharma; and also being able to leave behind attachment to the sense pleasures of later lives, which can give rise to bad views. In this way what is trained becomes pure and excellent. 'Make no effort over others' faults, and be at ease; always examine your own faults, and having recognised them, quickly confess them': this verse shows leaving behind the intention to seek out other people's faults; being undistracted in one's own wholesome qualities and always glad; knowing one's own faults as they are, confessing and repenting of them, and being free from overestimation. For these reasons the training becomes pure. 'If you commit an offence, make amends for it in accordance with the Dharma; in whatever tasks should be done, be energetic and do them yourself': this verse shows making amends for offences and being able to leave behind greed for others' service and attendance. For these reasons the training becomes pure. 'In the Buddha and his disciples, their majesty and their teaching, have faith in all of it; see the great wrong and do not slander': this verse shows that the training becomes pure because faith is complete and because one sees great wrong in slandering. 'In the most profound dharmas, in what cannot be fathomed by thought, be able to give up the doctrines of your old teachers and do not cling firmly to your own views': this verse shows purity and excellence through leaving behind abiding in clinging to one's own views. 'Always delight in dwelling in seclusion, and in remote lodgings; constantly cultivate wholesome dharmas, with firm effort and courage': this verse shows that the means of the training in higher mind is excellent, because one is secluded in both body and mind; because one keeps to lodgings that favour concentration; because one leaves behind all unwholesome thoughts and cultivates only pure wholesome dharmas; because one is not overcome by secondary afflictions such as sinking and excitement; and because one can fully complete right application. 'Without desire, yet generating desire; without aversion, yet having aversion; free from sleep, yet sleeping; at times not dwelling in quiet; free from regret, yet regretting; without longing, yet longing; in every way and at all times, accomplishing right means': these two verses show that the training in higher mind becomes ever purer because one leaves behind the hindrances of sensual desire, ill will, lethargy and drowsiness, restlessness and regret, and doubt; because one generates desire for wholesome dharmas; because one is deeply averse to sense pleasures; because, so as to be fit for the application of cultivating wholesome qualities and to keep the mind calm, one sleeps at the proper times; because, when the mind sinks or one fears it may, one attends to a pure and beautiful sign, and when walking about one does not stay in quiet; because one feels regret for offences committed before, and no regret for what one has not committed; because one longs for ever higher attainment; and because one's right means are earnest and uninterrupted. 'Drawing forth, awakening, binding through union, having signs, intimacy, many kinds of delight, pressing, and extreme intimacy: these are called false discriminations; they produce sensual lust, and the wise should leave them behind': these two verses show the eight kinds of false discrimination that produce craving for sexual desire, arising in order from the first preparation to its completion. By leaving them behind, all that is trained becomes pure and excellent. 'Drawing-forth discrimination' is the discrimination of a mind associated with incorrect reflection that draws forth an attractive object. 'Awakening discrimination' is the discrimination, associated with the entanglement of greed, that awakens to that attractive object. 'Discrimination bound through union' is the discrimination concerning that attractive object. 'Discrimination having signs' is the discrimination that grasps the various pure and beautiful features of that attractive object. 'Intimacy discrimination' is the discrimination associated with eagerness towards the beloved object once obtained. 'Delight discrimination' is the discrimination that proceeds in various ways, longing for and delighting in the many ways of enjoying what has been obtained. 'Pressing discrimination' is the discrimination at the time the two organs meet. 'Extreme-intimacy discrimination' is the discrimination at the time the impure fluid is emitted. 'Sense pleasures are never satisfying, shared by many, a cause of what is not Dharma; they increase craving, should be left behind by the wise and noble, quickly go to ruin, rely on many conditions, and are the ground of danger and heedlessness': these two verses show eight dangers of sense pleasures, in this life and the next, as appropriate. Seeing them is the means of cutting off desire for sense pleasures. 'Sense pleasures are like a dry bone, like a piece of soft flesh, like a grass torch, like a great pit of fire, like a venomous snake, like what is seen in a dream, like borrowed ornaments, like ripe fruit at the top of a tree. Knowing sense pleasures in this way, one should not delight in them at all': here, for the eight dangers in sense pleasures stated above, such as never being satisfying, similes accepted by the whole world are cited at length to show how deep and heavy the dangers of sense pleasures are. It also shows that, since sense pleasures so clearly have these many dangers, what wise person would delight in them? Further, sense pleasures are never satisfying, as a dry bone is; shared by many, as a piece of flesh is; a cause of what is not Dharma, as a grass torch is, because it burns fiercely the moment it is lit; they increase craving, as a great pit of fire does, because they produce thirst; the wise and noble leave them behind, as they would venom; they quickly go to ruin, as what is seen in a dream does; they rely on many conditions, as borrowed ornaments do; they are the ground of danger, ruin, and heedlessness, as over-ripe fruit at the top of a tree is. 'One should listen to the true Dharma and always reflect and cultivate; first see the coarse and the calm, then cultivate single-mindedly; give up the coarse burden of the afflictions and delight in abandonment; examine the signs, reach the completion of application; leave behind the desire of the desire realm and the desire of the form realm; enter the direct realisation of the truths, leave behind all desire, realise nirvana in this present life, and the final exhaustion of the remainder': this shows that, through the seven attentions beginning with the attention that discerns characteristics, both the worldly and world-transcending paths are purified; one realises the two fruits of nirvana, with remainder and without remainder, and the training in higher wisdom is ultimately purified. The words 'listen to the true Dharma and always reflect' show the attention that discerns characteristics. 'Always cultivate' shows the attention of conviction, because one cultivates by generating conviction. 'First see the coarse and the calm' shows the attention of seclusion. 'Cultivate single-mindedly' and so on shows the attention that gathers joy. 'Examine the signs' shows the attention of examination. 'Completion of application' shows the attention of completing application. The words 'leave behind the desire of the desire realm and the desire of the form realm; enter the direct realisation of the truths; leave behind all desire', and so on, show the attention of the fruit of completing application, worldly and world-transcending.

items.zh: 已釋意趣義聖教伽他。今當建立體義伽他。如頌言：
items.en: The verses on essential intent have now been explained. Now the verses on the essential body of the teaching should be established. [The commentarial gloss (披尋記) explains:] Proclaiming the Dharma's essentials is called the body; disclosing its underlying meaning is called its significance. A summary verse states: evil, teaching, craving, flow, dread, kind, renown, pool, flow, craving, action, toil, attainment of benefit, and discourse — fourteen topics in all.

items.zh: 於身語意諸所有一切世間惡莫作，由念正知、離諸欲，勿親能引無義苦。
items.en: Whatever belongs to body, speech, and mind — let none of the world's evil be done; through mindfulness and clear comprehension, abandon every desire; do not draw close to what brings suffering devoid of benefit.

items.zh: 今此頌中，所言惡者，謂諸惡行。於一切種、一切因緣、一切處所所有惡行。皆不應作。云何於一切種不作惡耶？謂由身語意不造眾惡故。云何於一切因緣不作惡耶？謂由貪瞋癡所生諸惡終不造作故。云何於一切處所不作惡耶？謂依有情事處及非有情事處不造眾惡故。
items.en: In this verse, "evil" refers to evil conduct of every kind. Evil should never be done in any type, from any cause, or in any place whatsoever. What is meant by not doing evil in any type? Never producing evil through body, speech, or mind. What is meant by not doing evil from any cause? Never producing the evils that arise from craving, aversion, and delusion. What is meant by not doing evil in any place? Never producing evil in relation to sentient beings or to non-sentient things.

items.zh: 云何由念正知遠離諸欲？謂斷事欲及斷煩惱欲故。云何斷事欲？謂如有一，於如來所證正法毘柰耶中得清淨信，了知居家迫迮，猶如牢獄，思求出離，廣說乃至由正信心，捨離家法，趣入非家，然於欲貪猶未永離。
items.en: What is meant by abandoning desire through mindfulness and clear comprehension? It means severing desire's objects and severing desire's affliction. What is severing desire's objects? It means one who, gaining pure faith in the Dharma and discipline realised by the Tathāgata, recognises household life to be as confining as a prison, and seeks to leave it... through this pure faith, one abandons household life and enters homelessness — though the craving of desire is not yet entirely gone.
This is called cutting off desire for objects.

items.zh: 云何斷煩惱欲？謂彼既出家已，為令欲貪無餘斷故，往趣曠野山林，安居邊際臥具，或住阿練若處，乃至或在空閑靜室。於諸事欲所起一切煩惱欲攝妄分別貪，為對治故，修四念住。
items.en: What is severing desire's affliction? It means that, having gone forth, in order to eliminate craving entirely, one goes to a wilderness or forest, settles with the most minimal bedding, dwells in a secluded place, or in a quiet, empty room; and in order to counteract every affliction of desire — every false conception of craving arising in connection with desire's objects — one cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness.

items.zh: 或復還出，依近聚落、村邑而住，善護其身、善守諸根、善住正念而入聚落。或復村邑遊行旋反，去來進止恒住正知，為解睡眠及諸勞倦。彼即於是四念住中，善安正念為依止故；為欲永斷欲貪隨眠，修習對治。
items.en: Or else they come out again and live near towns and villages, guarding their bodies well, guarding their senses well, abiding well in right mindfulness as they enter the village. Or, walking about the villages and returning, they always keep clear awareness in going and coming, moving and stopping, to dispel drowsiness and fatigue. Relying on right mindfulness well established in these four foundations of mindfulness, they cultivate the antidote in order to cut off for ever the latent tendency of sensual lust.

items.title: Topic One Closes: Freedom From Desire's Fruit, and the Harm of Self-Torment

items.zh: 又即以彼正知而住為依止故，遠離諸蓋，身心調暢，有所堪能，熾然方便修斷寂靜。彼由如是念及正知為依止故，便能證得煩惱欲斷，遠離諸欲，乃至於初靜慮具足而住。
items.en: And, resting on that same abiding in clear comprehension, one becomes free of the hindrances; body and mind grow pliant and capable, and one applies oneself with ardent effort to cultivating their cessation, and to stillness. Resting on mindfulness and clear comprehension in this way, one is able to realise the severing of desire's affliction, becoming free of desire, up to and including dwelling fully in the first meditative absorption.

items.zh: 如是能於受用欲樂行邊，劣、鄙、穢性諸異生法、若斷若知。
items.en: In this way they can abandon and understand the base, vulgar, and impure dharmas of ordinary beings found in the extreme of indulging in sense pleasures.

items.zh: 何等名為引無義苦？謂如有一，若諸沙門或婆羅門，行自苦行，於現法中，以種種苦自逼自切，周遍燒惱。自謂我今由現法苦所逼惱故，解脫當苦。雖求是事而自煎逼，彼於此事終不能得，然更招集大損惱事。
items.en: What is meant by bringing on suffering devoid of benefit? It refers to one — whether an ascetic or a brahmin — who practices self-torment, afflicting and scourging themselves in every way in this very life, thinking: through the suffering that afflicts me now, I will be freed from future suffering. Though seeking this goal, and tormenting themselves in pursuit of it, they never actually attain it — and instead bring upon themselves great further harm.
This is called bringing on pointless suffering.

items.zh: 諸聖弟子，能於如是受用自苦行邊能引非聖無義苦法善了知已，遠而避之，不親、不近、亦不承事。
items.en: The noble disciples, having thoroughly understood this practice of self-torment as an ignoble teaching bringing suffering devoid of benefit, keep their distance from it, neither drawing close to it, nor associating with it, nor paying homage to those who practice it.

items.title: Topic One's Summary: Two Kinds of Fulfilment Every Being Seeks

items.zh: 復次，今當略辯上所說義。云何略辯？謂諸有情有二種滿。一、增上生滿，二、決定勝滿。增上生滿者，謂往善趣。決定勝滿者，謂愛盡、離欲、寂滅、涅槃。於此二滿及與障礙，能斷能證，是名略義。
items.en: Furthermore, let what has been said above now be briefly explained. What is this brief explanation? It is that sentient beings seek two kinds of fulfilment: first, the fulfilment of a favourable rebirth; and second, the fulfilment of decisive excellence. The fulfilment of a favourable rebirth means proceeding to a good realm of rebirth. The fulfilment of decisive excellence means the exhaustion of craving, freedom from desire, cessation, and nirvāṇa. Being able to sever the obstacles to, and realise, both of these fulfillments — this is the brief explanation.

items.zh: 若於一切種、一切因緣、一切處所不作惡行，彼便能斷增上生滿所有障礙，亦能證得增上生滿。若於受用欲樂行邊及於受用自苦行邊決定遠離，彼便能斷決定勝滿所有障礙，亦能證得決定勝滿。當知是名此中略義。
items.en: If one refrains from evil conduct of every type, from every cause, in every place, one thereby severs every obstacle to the fulfilment of a favourable rebirth, and also realises that fulfilment. If one resolutely keeps clear of both the indulgence of sensual pleasure and the practice of self-torment, one thereby severs every obstacle to the fulfilment of decisive excellence, and also realises that fulfilment. Know that this is the brief explanation given here.

blocks.text: Now the third kind of verse: the **verses of essential body** (體義伽他), which tell the practitioner what to do. They are drawn from conversations between the Buddha and devas, and each is followed by an explanation. Ru-Yi's English resumes, with short omissions marked.

"Let none of the world's evil be done": evil should never be done "in any type, from any cause, or in any place": through body, speech, or mind; from greed, hatred, or delusion; towards beings or things. Master Cháng Bǎi links the verse to the well-known lines: "Do no evil, practise all good, purify one's own mind: this is the teaching of all buddhas."

The treatise distinguishes **desire as object** (事欲) and **desire as affliction** (煩惱欲). Going forth severs the objects; one recognises household life to be "as confining as a prison". But, the treatise says frankly, the craving is not yet gone. Master Cháng Bǎi: wherever desire's objects are present, the affliction is present too; but the affliction may be present without the objects. Hence the renunciant goes on to the wilderness to practise the four foundations of mindfulness.

"Through mindfulness and clear comprehension": Master Cháng Bǎi reads the character 念 as "present mind" (今心); when this present thought accords with the Dharma, it is right mindfulness. Venerable Miào Jìng: if one notices at once that the mind has strayed, that noticing is clear comprehension.

Some believe that the suffering they inflict on themselves now will free them from future suffering. They never attain it, and do themselves great harm. Venerable Miào Jìng: freedom from suffering comes from wisdom of the true nature of things, "not from enduring suffering". The noble disciples neither associate with nor honour such practices.

The brief meaning: every being seeks two fulfilments: of **a favourable rebirth** and of **decisive excellence**, that is, "the exhaustion of craving, freedom from desire, cessation, nirvāṇa". Venerable Miào Jìng distinguishes "craving" (愛) for future things from "desire" (欲) for present ones. Avoiding the extreme of indulgence and the extreme of self-torment, one reaches both fulfilments: the middle way of the first sermon, here in Yogācāra form.

quiz.q: The first verse says "let none of the world's evil be done." In which three respects does the treatise say evil should never be done?
options: past, present, and future
the desire, form, and formless realms
every type, every cause, every place — body, speech, and mind; what arises from craving, aversion, and delusion; sentient beings and non-sentient things
towards parents, teachers, and the Three Jewels
quiz.why: "Evil should never be done in any type, from any cause, or in any place whatsoever." Every type means the three doors of body, speech, and mind; every cause means the three roots of craving, aversion, and delusion; every place means sentient beings and non-sentient things. Master Cháng Bǎi's examples: killing is evil done in relation to sentient beings; stealing property is evil done in relation to non-sentient things.

quiz.q: Which famous verse does Master Cháng Bǎi use to sum up the essence of the first verse?
options: the verse common to the seven buddhas: "Do no evil, practice all good, purify one's own mind — this is the teaching of all buddhas"
"all conditioned things are impermanent"
"all conditioned things are like a dream"
"give rise to a mind that abides nowhere"
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "The essence of the Buddha's teaching is: do no evil, practice all good, purify one's own mind — this is the teaching of all buddhas." The verse's "let none of the world's evil be done" is exactly the first line, while "through mindfulness and clear comprehension, abandon every desire" corresponds to purifying one's own mind.

quiz.q: On "through mindfulness and clear comprehension," how do the two masters distinguish mindfulness from clear comprehension?
options: Cháng Bǎi: 念 is "the present mind," and a present thought in accord with the Dharma is right mindfulness; Miào Jìng: immediately noticing when mindfulness has slipped onto what should not be thought of is clear comprehension
they are identical
mindfulness is concentration, clear comprehension is precepts
mindfulness is Mahāyāna, clear comprehension is Hīnayāna
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: the character 念 is "present mind"; when this present thought is correct and accords with the true Dharma, it is right mindfulness. Venerable Miào Jìng: if mindfulness is lost and the mind dwells on what it should not, one must notice at once — that noticing is clear comprehension.

quiz.q: According to Master Cháng Bǎi, how are desire's objects and desire's affliction related?
options: where there is desire for objects there is always the affliction of desire, but the affliction can be present without the objects
they are unrelated
the affliction always comes with objects
severing the objects automatically severs the affliction
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: of course, wherever desire's objects are present, desire's affliction is present too; but the affliction may be present without the objects. That is why, having severed the objects by going forth, one still goes to the wilderness to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness against the affliction — false conceptions of craving.

quiz.q: Why, per Venerable Miào Jìng, can self-torment not free one from suffering?
options: the austerity is too light
there is no teacher
it is not practised long enough
only the wisdom of the true nature of phenomena frees one from suffering, not enduring suffering itself
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: to be free of this suffering one must attain wisdom of the true nature of phenomena; it is not that enduring suffering frees one from suffering. He also glosses "bringing on": the suffering was not there originally — one deliberately draws it out oneself.

quiz.q: What two kinds of fulfilment does the treatise say sentient beings have?
options: merit and wisdom
favourable rebirth — going to a good realm; decisive excellence — exhaustion of craving, freedom from desire, cessation, nirvāṇa
self-benefit and benefit of others
precepts and concentration
quiz.why: "The fulfilment of a favourable rebirth means proceeding to a good realm of rebirth. The fulfilment of decisive excellence means the exhaustion of craving, freedom from desire, cessation, and nirvāṇa." Severing the obstacles to both and realising both is the brief explanation.

quiz.q: How does Venerable Miào Jìng distinguish the "craving" in exhaustion of craving from the "desire" in freedom from desire?
options: craving is sexual, desire is for property
they are synonyms
craving is for laypeople, desire for monastics
craving concerns lovable things in the future; desire concerns what one loves now
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "craving" is said of lovable things in the future; "desire" refers to present things — what one loves now is called desire. So exhaustion of craving is no longer seeking future existence, and freedom from desire is no longer delighting in present objects.
